<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1280 720" width="1280" height="720">
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="720" fill="#FFFFFF"/>
  <defs>
    <linearGradient id="topBar" x1="0%" y1="0%" x2="100%" y2="0%">
      <stop offset="0%" stop-color="#0D47A1"/>
      <stop offset="100%" stop-color="#42A5F5"/>
    </linearGradient>
  </defs>
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="1280" height="4" fill="url(#topBar)"/>
  <!-- Title -->
  <text x="60" y="50" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="28" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Key Takeaways: Bigger Pages, Smarter Protocols, Stronger Security</text>

  <!-- 5 takeaway items with icon bullets -->
  <!-- Item 1 -->
  <rect x="60" y="85" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#F5F7FA"/>
  <use data-icon="arrow-trend-up" x="80" y="105" width="32" height="32" fill="#E65100"/>
  <text x="130" y="115" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Page Weight Keeps Climbing</text>
  <text x="130" y="140" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">Median desktop pages now transfer ~2,000 KB — roughly 25% heavier than in 2020,</text>
  <text x="130" y="160" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">driven by richer media and JavaScript payloads.</text>

  <!-- Item 2 -->
  <rect x="60" y="185" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E0E0E0" stroke-width="1"/>
  <use data-icon="shield-check" x="80" y="205" width="32" height="32" fill="#2E7D32"/>
  <text x="130" y="215" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">HTTPS Is the New Baseline</text>
  <text x="130" y="240" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">At 99%+ of requests, unencrypted HTTP is essentially extinct on the modern web.</text>
  <text x="130" y="260" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">Desktop: 99.2% | Mobile: 99.1%</text>

  <!-- Item 3 -->
  <rect x="60" y="285" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#F5F7FA"/>
  <use data-icon="globe" x="80" y="305" width="32" height="32" fill="#0D47A1"/>
  <text x="130" y="315" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">HTTP/3 Is the Fastest-Growing Protocol Metric</text>
  <text x="130" y="340" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">From near-zero to ~40% support in under four years, HTTP/3 is rapidly becoming</text>
  <text x="130" y="360" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">mainstream. Desktop: 38.7% | Mobile: 40.0%</text>

  <!-- Item 4 -->
  <rect x="60" y="385" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#FFFFFF" stroke="#E0E0E0" stroke-width="1"/>
  <use data-icon="arrow-trend-down" x="80" y="405" width="32" height="32" fill="#1565C0"/>
  <text x="130" y="415" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Fewer TCP Connections Despite More Requests</text>
  <text x="130" y="440" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">Multiplexing in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 has cut median connections per page by 15–27%,</text>
  <text x="130" y="460" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">improving network efficiency.</text>

  <!-- Item 5 -->
  <rect x="60" y="485" width="1160" height="88" rx="10" fill="#F5F7FA"/>
  <use data-icon="font-case" x="80" y="505" width="32" height="32" fill="#E65100"/>
  <text x="130" y="515" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#212121">Font-Display Still Underused</text>
  <text x="130" y="540" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">At ~40–42% adoption, there is significant room for improvement in avoiding</text>
  <text x="130" y="560" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="16" fill="#616161">invisible text during font loading.</text>

  <!-- Call to action -->
  <rect x="60" y="600" width="1160" height="60" rx="10" fill="#0D47A1" fill-opacity="0.06"/>
  <use data-icon="target" x="80" y="614" width="32" height="32" fill="#0D47A1"/>
  <text x="130" y="630" font-family="Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="bold" fill="#0D47A1">Benchmark your sites against these baselines using HTTP Archive data at httparchive.org</text>
  <text x="130" y="650" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="14" fill="#616161">Run WebPageTest, Lighthouse, or CrUX queries to see where you stand relative to global trends.</text>

  <!-- Footer -->
  <text x="60" y="700" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#9E9E9E">Source: HTTP Archive — State of the Web Report</text>
  <text x="1220" y="700" font-family="Calibri, Arial, sans-serif" font-size="11" fill="#9E9E9E" text-anchor="end">8 / 8</text>
</svg>

arguments.content:
# 01_cover

Welcome to our deep dive into the State of the Web from 2020 through 2025. This presentation draws entirely from HTTP Archive data — a continuous crawl of millions of URLs that records how the web is actually built.

Over the next twenty minutes, we will walk through five macro-level trends: page weight growth, request and connection efficiency, HTTPS adoption, the HTTP/2-to-HTTP/3 protocol shift, and font-display CSS adoption. [Pause]

Our goal is to equip you with concrete baselines so you can benchmark your own sites against these industry-wide trends.

Key points: ① Data source is HTTP Archive's State of the Web report ② Time range covers January 2020 through March 2026 ③ All metrics split by desktop and mobile
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 02_sample_size

[Transition] Before we look at what the data tells us, let's understand how much data we are actually working with.

The HTTP Archive crawl has tripled in size since 2020. Desktop URLs went from roughly five million to sixteen million, and mobile from three-and-a-half million to twelve-and-a-half million. [Data] That sharp jump you see around mid-2022 reflects a major expansion of the crawl infrastructure. Since mid-2023, the sample has plateaued, giving us a stable and increasingly representative view of the web. [Pause]

This larger sample means the trends we are about to review are grounded in significantly more data than earlier reports.

Key points: ① Desktop ~5M to ~16M URLs ② Mobile ~3.5M to ~12.5M URLs ③ Sharp expansion mid-2022, stable since mid-2023
Duration: 2 minutes

---

# 03_page_weight

[Transition] With that robust sample in place, let's look at what it reveals about page weight.

Median desktop pages now weigh approximately two thousand kilobytes — roughly twenty-five percent heavier than in early 2020. Mobile tracks slightly below at around nineteen hundred kilobytes but follows the same upward trajectory. [Data] The seventy-fifth percentile on desktop exceeds four thousand kilobytes, indicating a long tail of very heavy pages. [Pause]

This growth is driven primarily by richer media assets and increasing JavaScript payloads. If your median page is significantly above two thousand KB, you are heavier than the industry norm.

Key points: ① Desktop median ~1,600 KB to ~2,000 KB (▲ ~25%) ② Mobile tracks slightly lower ③ P75 desktop exceeds 4,000 KB — long tail of heavy pages
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 04_requests_connections

[Transition] More bytes mean more resources — but interestingly, request counts have grown only modestly while the number of TCP connections has actually dropped.

The median desktop page makes seventy-six requests, up just two-point-seven percent. Mobile sits at seventy-one, up two-point-nine percent. Meanwhile, TCP connections per page have fallen from about fifteen to twelve on desktop — a fourteen percent drop — and from fifteen to eleven on mobile, a twenty-seven percent drop. [Pause]

[Data] This is the multiplexing dividend from HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Multiple requests flow over fewer connections, reducing connection setup overhead and improving network efficiency.

Key points: ① Desktop 76 requests (▲ 2.7%), Mobile 71 (▲ 2.9%) ② TCP connections: desktop 15 → 12 (▼ 14.3%), mobile 15 → 11 (▼ 26.7%) ③ Multiplexing in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 is the driver
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 05_https_adoption

[Transition] While protocols have gotten more efficient, they have also gotten dramatically more secure.

HTTPS adoption is now effectively universal. [Data] Ninety-nine-point-two percent of desktop requests and ninety-nine-point-one percent of mobile requests use HTTPS. That is up roughly nineteen to twenty percentage points from 2020, when adoption was around eighty percent. [Pause]

Plaintext HTTP is essentially extinct on the modern web. If you still have any HTTP-only resources in your stack, you are in a vanishing minority. This shift was driven by browser warnings, Let's Encrypt, and CDN default-on encryption.

Key points: ① Desktop 99.2%, Mobile 99.1% HTTPS ② Up ~19–20 percentage points since 2020 ③ Unencrypted HTTP is effectively gone
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 06_http2_http3

[Transition] HTTPS is the security baseline — now let's look at what is happening at the protocol layer above it.

HTTP/2 accounts for about fifty-eight-point-six percent of desktop requests and fifty-seven-point-six percent on mobile. Growth here has been modest — one to three percent recently — because HTTP/3 is absorbing much of the newer adoption. [Pause]

[Data] HTTP/3 support has gone from near-zero to roughly forty percent in under four years — the fastest-growing metric in this entire report. An important caveat: HTTP Archive measures HTTP/3 support via Alt-Svc headers, not actual usage, because fresh Chrome instances default to HTTP/2 on first connection.

Key points: ① HTTP/2: ~58–59% of requests, growth plateauing ② HTTP/3: ~39–40% support, explosive growth from near-zero ③ Measurement caveat — support vs. actual usage
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 07_font_display

[Transition] Shifting from protocols to performance best practices, let's look at font-display CSS adoption.

The font-display property helps avoid the Flash of Invisible Text — FOIT — during web font loading. As measured by Lighthouse, forty-point-one percent of desktop pages and forty-two-point-five percent of mobile pages now use this property. [Data] Mobile adoption has grown sixty-one percent since 2020, far outpacing desktop's fourteen-point-nine percent growth. [Pause]

Despite this progress, more than half of all pages still risk FOIT. Adding font-display swap to your CSS font-face declarations is one of the simplest performance wins available today.

Key points: ① Desktop 40.1%, Mobile 42.5% adoption ② Mobile growth 61.0% since 2020, desktop 14.9% ③ Over half of pages still risk FOIT — significant room for improvement
Duration: 2.5 minutes

---

# 08_key_takeaways

[Transition] Let me bring this all together with five key takeaways.

First, page weight keeps climbing — median desktop pages are about twenty-five percent heavier than in 2020. Second, HTTPS is the new baseline at ninety-nine percent plus. Third, HTTP/3 is the fastest-growing protocol metric, going from near-zero to forty percent in four years. Fourth, multiplexing has cut TCP connections by fifteen to twenty-seven percent despite more requests. And fifth, font-display adoption at roughly forty percent still has substantial room to grow. [Pause]

My call to action: benchmark your own sites against these baselines. Use HTTP Archive data, run WebPageTest and Lighthouse audits, and query CrUX to see where you stand relative to these global trends. The data is open and free — take advantage of it.

Key points: ① Five macro trends summarized ② All metrics referenced from HTTP Archive data ③ Call to action: benchmark against these baselines at httparchive.org
Duration: 3 minutes

The final presentation has been saved to `/app/output/final_deck.pptx` (71 KB, 8 slides, native DrawingML shapes with speaker notes and fade transitions).

**Deck summary:**
1. Title slide with HTTP Archive source and time range
2. Crawl sample size — dual-line time-series (desktop/mobile)
3. Page weight trends — area chart with IQR band
4. Requests & connections — split layout with stat cards + declining line chart
5. HTTPS at 99%+ — large stat callout + time-series
6. HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 — grouped bars + HTTP/3 rapid-rise inset
7. Font-display adoption — stat cards + stacked bars
8. Key takeaways — 5 findings + benchmark call to action
